newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ex-Nomura chief arrested over racketeer scandal.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nomura chief arrested over racketeer scandal.

text.p: Former Nomura Securities president Hideo Sakamaki was arrested on Friday in a widening payoff scandal, as Japanese leaders vowed to clean up the financial sector and restore confidence at home and abroad.

Tokyo prosecutors said Sakamaki, who stepped down as president in March over the scandal, was suspected of conspiring with three Nomura executives to pay 38.5 million yen ($331,000) in 1995 to Ryuichi Koike, a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer at the heart of the affair.

The deepening scandal has tarnished the reputation of Japanese business, as well as slashing Nomura's profits. It is also testing the resolve of authorities to punish misdeeds and tighten surveillance as they cut the web of rules that have kept Tokyo's financial firms wrapped in a protective cocoon.

"The government wants a no-holds-barred, full-fledged investigation into the scandal to restore public confidence in the entire securities industry," said Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama. "We want this arrest to bring about sound management in the securities industry.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Friday that Sakamaki's arrest would have a severe effect on the country's securities industry, Kyodo news agency reported.
"It is not important whether or not he was arrested. What matters is that the leader of a top-ranking company has caused a problem like this," he was quoted as saying.

The scandal is the second to hit Nomura, Japan's biggest brokerage, in six years. It has also ensnared Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd, one of Japan's biggest banks, which is also being probed by prosecutors.

The arrest of Sakamaki, who became president after scandals in 1991 forced his predecessor to resign, was a particularly harsh blow to Nomura's reputation, since the company had said that management involvement in the wrongdoing was limited to two executives arrested earlier this month.

Junichi Ujiie, who took over as Nomura president on May 1 as part of a sweeping management shake-up, on Friday conceded that Sakamaki's arrest raised suspicions that the company itself played a part in the scandal, although he added that not all Nomura executives and officials were involved.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka dubbed the fresh arrest "very grave and beyond words".

He said he would urge the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) to push ahead with its probe of Nomura and added the ministry would take stern steps after receiving the watchdog's recommendations.
"The fact that the government and the prosecutors are acting sternly (on the scandal) will gain understanding overseas," Mitsuzuka said.

The SESC earlier this month filed a complaint with prosecutors against Nomura, two former Nomura executives and a company official alleging they had illegally compensated a firm run by Koike's younger brother Yoshinori. Prosecutors then arrested the two former Nomura executives and the company official as well as the Koike brothers.
No formal charges have yet been brought in the case.
Sokaiya are racketeers who buy stakes in firms and extort money by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings.
Payoffs to sokaiya were banned under a revision to Japan's Commercial Code in 1982. Those violating the law face a fine of up to 300,000 yen ($2,586) or up to six months in jail.
Compensating investors' losses is also banned under the Securities and Exchange Law, which was revised after brokerage scandals in 1991.

Prosecutors said they believed the cash was handed over on March 15, 1995 as a "token of appreciation" for Koike's future cooperation in ensuring the brokerage's annual shareholders' meeting, held the following June, went smoothly.
Japanese Finance Ministry officials, their own image tarnished by a series of policy missteps in recent years, are also in the hot seat over the scandal.

Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank admitted last Friday that it might have hidden improper loans to the younger Koike and his company from ministry inspections. Critics charge that the ministry should have uncovered the dubious loans, but officials say this is all but impossible if banks try to hide them.
On Thursday, parliament's Lower House passed a bill to set up a new government agency, separate from the Finance Ministry, to police the scandal-tainted financial sector. ($1=116 yen)
